name: backup
title: A backup script
pitch: Disks die and files get deleted by mistake. You'll write a script that saves a folder into dated archives, keeps only the last few, runs every day on its own, and can bring a file back.

steps.do: Create a test folder with a few files and subfolders.
steps.hint: `mkdir -p test/a/b`, then `echo` some text into a few files.
steps.why: A small folder you know by heart makes it easy to check that a backup holds everything.

steps.do: Pack the folder into one archive with tar.
steps.hint: `tar -czf backup.tar.gz test`: c to create, z to compress, f for the file name.
steps.why: tar turns a whole tree of files into one file, keeping names, folders and permissions. That's why backups and software downloads use it.

steps.do: List what's inside the archive without unpacking it.
steps.done: you see every file of the folder.
steps.why: A backup you never checked is a hope, not a backup. Listing is the quick check.

steps.do: Give the archive a dated name, like backup-2026-10-02.tar.gz.
steps.hint: `$(date +%F)` puts today's date into a command.
steps.why: Dated names keep several backups side by side and sort in time order. %F writes the date as year-month-day, which sorts correctly as text.

steps.do: Put it in a script that takes the folder to save and the destination folder as arguments.
steps.done: `./backup.sh ~/test ~/backups` works, and a missing argument prints how to use it.
steps.hint: Start from the template (lesson Your first script): `$1` and `$2`, and `(( $# == 2 )) || usage` to check you got both, with a usage() that prints `usage: backup.sh FOLDER DEST` on stderr and exits 2.
steps.why: Arguments let the same script back up any folder anywhere. Checking them first stops a typo from becoming a strange error further down.

steps.do: Keep only the last 5 backups: delete the older ones.
steps.done: after 7 runs, only the 5 newest archives are left.
steps.hint: Dated names sort in time order, and a glob gives them sorted: `backups=("$dest"/backup-*.tar.gz)`. All but the last 5 are `"${backups[@]:0:${#backups[@]}-5}"`, when there are more than 5: `rm --` them. Test with fake dates (`touch backup-2020-01-0{1..7}.tar.gz`).
steps.why: Backups that are never cleaned fill the disk, and then the next backup fails. Deleting is dangerous, so test this part with fake files first.

steps.do: Check every command: if tar fails (a full disk, a missing folder), the script says so and exits with an error code.
steps.done: a missing folder gives a clear message, and `echo $?` shows a code that isn't 0.
steps.hint: `tar … || die "backup failed"`, with the template's die: the message on stderr, then exit 1. Check each command that matters this way (lesson Errors in scripts). Write the archive as "$archive.part", and mv -- it to its real name only when tar worked: a broken archive never counts as one of the 5 kept.
steps.why: A backup that fails silently is the worst kind: you find out on the day you need it. Loud failures are a feature.

steps.do: Run it every day automatically, with cron or a systemd timer.
steps.done: a new archive appears the next day (or the next minute, for the test).
steps.hint: `crontab -e` and a line like `0 3 * * * /path/backup.sh …`. Use full paths: cron doesn't load your shell's settings.
steps.why: The best backup is the one you don't have to remember. Scheduled jobs run in a bare environment, which is why full paths matter there.

steps.do: Restore one file from a backup into another folder.
steps.done: the restored file is the same as the original: `diff` prints nothing.
steps.why: Restoring is the real test of a backup. Practising it before a disaster is what professionals do.

steps.do: Optional: exclude some files, or copy only what changed with rsync.
steps.done: the excluded files are not in the archive.
steps.why: Real backups skip caches and temporary files. Knowing rsync opens the door to backups on another machine.
